title: Vaupel (2010): True or False
instructions: Use the reading to evaluate each statement's scope, direction, and strength, then choose True or False.

items.prompt: Vaupel summarizes the central finding as a delay in human senescence of about a decade.
items.explanation: The abstract describes this finding as first documented in 1994 and strengthened by subsequent evidence available for the 2010 review.

items.prompt: The article attributes the postponement of mortality mainly to revolutionary success in slowing the rate of deterioration with age.
items.explanation: Vaupel attributes the observed progress to improving health and reaching old age in better condition, distinguishing postponement from a slower rate of aging.

items.prompt: In Figure 1, X5 and X10 rising along similar paths while remaining about a decade apart supports postponement of senescence.
items.explanation: The ages associated with five and ten years of remaining life expectancy shift together. Vaupel interprets this as postponement rather than lengthening of the deterioration process.

items.prompt: Figure 2 shows that extremely old women were rare roughly half a century earlier, followed by rapid increases in Swedish women aged 100+ and Japanese women aged 105+.
items.explanation: The two historical series show growing numbers at very old ages. They do not directly establish the health status of each person counted.

items.prompt: The estimate that genetic variation accounts for about 25% of adult lifespan variation means that genes fix exactly one quarter of each person's lifespan.
items.explanation: The Danish twin result concerns variation between individuals in a population. It does not divide an individual life into a genetically fixed fraction and a remaining fraction.

items.prompt: The review reports that several major human longevity genes with effects far larger than APOE had already been repeatedly verified.
items.explanation: Vaupel describes limited success in identifying major longevity genes and emphasizes the modest effects and limited replication of the findings available at the time.

items.prompt: The article concludes that years lived with disability consistently decreased across every country and every severity level.
items.explanation: Trends differed: years with the most severe disability tended to decrease, whereas years with less severe disability tended to increase, with substantial national variation.

items.prompt: Better diagnosis and treatment can increase morbidity prevalence by identifying more illness and allowing people to live longer with it.
items.explanation: Prevalence reflects incidence and survival. Rehabilitation can also reduce disability without eliminating the underlying illness.

items.prompt: The health–survival paradox means that older women appear healthier than men of the same age but die earlier.
items.explanation: The direction is reversed: older men generally appear healthier on several measures, yet die younger than women.

items.prompt: Among people with validated ages from 110 to 114, the review reports an approximately constant annual death probability of 50%.
items.explanation: The finding relies on age validation. Observations beyond age 114 were sparse, limiting claims about those later ages.

items.prompt: According to Box 1, a plateau in population mortality proves that every surviving individual has stopped aging.
items.explanation: Selective survival can change the composition of a population and flatten its aggregate mortality curve even while risk continues to rise within each subpopulation.

items.prompt: Because progress against one disease has limited effects on lifespan, advances against several diseases cannot reinforce one another.
items.explanation: Vaupel argues that disease-specific advances can act synergistically, especially when older people have multiple conditions.

items.prompt: Vaupel distinguishes behaviors that help a person outlive contemporaries from prosperity and medicine shaping the population's general longevity level.
items.explanation: The review explicitly separates relative individual longevity from the broader conditions determining longevity across a population.

items.prompt: The projection that most children born since 2000 in high-life-expectancy countries may reach 100 depends on continued historical rates of mortality improvement.
items.explanation: The article states that continuation of the past trend is a condition of the projection and remains a matter of debate.

items.prompt: The work-redistribution proposal seeks to maintain economic output by spreading work across more years with correspondingly fewer weekly hours over the life course.
items.explanation: Figure 4 illustrates a hypothetical redistribution that allows a different mixture of education, employment, childrearing, and leisure across longer lives.
